# The James Webb Space Telescope: Design, Instruments, and Purpose

## Introduction

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is a space-based astronomical observatory designed to observe the universe in infrared light. According to NASA, Webb launched on December 25, 2021, and orbits the Sun 1.5 million kilometers away from Earth at the second Lagrange point, or L2, using a segmented, gold-coated mirror to observe in infrared ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/)). Wikipedia corroborates the launch date, reporting that Webb was launched on 25 December 2021 on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou, French Guiana ([Wikipedia, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)). This report describes the telescope’s design, its four main science instruments, and its purpose. It draws primarily on NASA’s mission page, a public-domain source, and secondarily on the Wikipedia article, a CC BY-SA 4.0 source, prioritizing the NASA source for mission-level facts and using Wikipedia for technical specifications ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/); [Wikipedia, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)). The central finding is that JWST is engineered around infrared observation: its orbit, mirror, wavelength coverage, and instrument suite all support the collection and analysis of infrared light from astronomical sources ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/); [Wikipedia, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)).

## Design and Architecture

### Launch and Deployment

JWST was launched on December 25, 2021, according to NASA ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/)). Wikipedia specifies that the launch occurred on 25 December 2021 on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou, French Guiana ([Wikipedia, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)). These details establish the telescope’s operational start and the vehicle and site used to place it into space. The launch date is consistent across both sources, which increases confidence in the fact ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/); [Wikipedia, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)). The use of an Ariane 5 rocket and the Kourou launch site are technical details supplied by Wikipedia ([Wikipedia, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)). NASA does not mention the launch vehicle or site in the provided material, so the report attributes those specifics to Wikipedia ([Wikipedia, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)).

### Orbital Location at L2

NASA states that Webb orbits the Sun 1.5 million kilometers away from Earth at the second Lagrange point, or L2 ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/)). This orbital location is a defining feature of the mission’s design. The distance of 1.5 million kilometers places the observatory far from Earth, and the L2 point is the specific gravitational location described by NASA ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/)). The source does not explain the mechanics of L2 in the provided excerpt, but it identifies L2 as the orbit used for infrared observation ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/)). The combination of a distant orbit and an infrared-optimized mirror indicates that the observatory is designed to operate away from Earth’s immediate environment ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/)). In practical terms, the L2 orbit is the vantage point from which JWST conducts its astronomical observations ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/)).

### Primary Mirror

The primary mirror is one of the most important elements of JWST’s design. Wikipedia reports that Webb’s primary mirror is a 6.5 m (21 ft)-diameter gold-coated beryllium reflector with a collecting area of 25.4 m² ([Wikipedia, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)). NASA describes the mirror as segmented and gold-coated ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/)). Combining these sources, the mirror is a large, segmented, gold-coated beryllium reflector with a 6.5 m diameter and a 25.4 m² collecting area ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/); [Wikipedia, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)). The diameter of 6.5 m is equivalent to 21 ft, as Wikipedia notes ([Wikipedia, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)). The collecting area of 25.4 m² is a quantitative measure of the mirror’s light-gathering capability ([Wikipedia, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)). The segmented design, reported by NASA, means the mirror is not a single continuous piece ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/)). The gold coating, reported by both sources, is a design feature of the reflecting surface ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/); [Wikipedia, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)). The use of beryllium as the mirror material is specified by Wikipedia ([Wikipedia, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)). These design choices are central to the telescope’s infrared capability ([NASA, 2026](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/)).
